inputs.title: The Thing
inputs.logline: When Bo’s big tail betrays how hard it is to meet new friends, Keen and Aida help him discover that the very thing he wants to hide may be the first thing everyone loves.

orderedEvents.text: Golden morning light. Dew sparkles on wildflowers. A honeycomb sits on a small stump. KEEN tiptoes toward it. He lifts his knees high with every step.
CRUNCH. CRUNCH. CRUNCH.
Keen freezes each time. He spots the honeycomb. His eyes widen. He LICKS HIS LIPS. He reaches toward the honey. FUZZBY the bee is asleep on top of the honeycomb.

orderedEvents.speaker: Fuzzby
orderedEvents.text: ZZZZZ …
A small snore bubble grows from his nose. Keen reaches closer to the honey. POP! The bubble bursts. Keen FREEZES.

orderedEvents.speaker: Fuzzby
orderedEvents.text: ZZZZZ …
Another bubble slowly grows. Keen inches closer to the honey.
POP! The second bubble bursts.

beats.storyBeat: Keen attempts an exaggerated stealth mission toward Fuzzby’s honeycomb, but every crunchy step and snore-bubble pop makes the world more awake than he wants it to be. The beat is about borrowed boldness meeting tiny physical resistance.
beats.want: Keen wants to get close enough to take honey without waking Fuzzby.
beats.need: He needs to learn that rushing toward what he wants is not the same as being ready or unseen.
beats.kidRead: Keen is being silly-sneaky and the sleeping bee might wake up any second.
beats.adultRead: A child’s confidence is charmingly exposed by his own body and the environment; he is not as invisible as he thinks.
beats.emotionalIntent: Light suspense and giggly anticipation, with the honeycomb as the forbidden prize.

beats.adultRead: The comedy is the impossibility of controlling every tell; Keen’s cover is doomed because he is still a kid in a too-big plan.
beats.emotionalIntent: Build the laugh through anticipation, release it with the sneeze, then button it with Fuzzby’s sleepy authority.

beats.need: She needs to trust the quiet signal and make room for someone else’s fear without taking over.
beats.kidRead: A magic bowl shows a squirrel who keeps packing but does not go anywhere.
beats.adultRead: The repetition is instantly recognizable as a child trying to make a hard transition feel controllable.
beats.emotionalIntent: Quiet wonder with a small ache under it; the vision should feel intimate, not flashy.

beats.storyBeat: Inside the hollow tree, Bo answers his offscreen Mum but bargains with time and his conker, delaying the Learning Circle by making “a minute” stretch absurdly. The safe room is cosy, but it is also a trap of postponement.
beats.want: Bo wants to put off leaving while sounding like he still intends to go.
beats.need: He needs to be witnessed in the stuck place instead of left alone with the loop.
beats.kidRead: Bo keeps finding reasons not to go yet, and his conker is like his little helper.
beats.adultRead: The offscreen parent call captures the morning-transition ache: encouragement from another room cannot cross the threshold for him.
beats.emotionalIntent: Tender comic avoidance; keep it small, domestic and recognisable.

vision.premise: Bo is due at the Learning Circle for the first time, but every step toward the door makes his tail poof with worry. Keen’s playful curiosity and Aida’s quiet truth help him move toward the group one step at a time, until the tail he feared becomes his way in.
vision.dramaticQuestion: Can Bo go to the Learning Circle without having to hide the part of himself that gives him away?
vision.theme: Belonging begins when the thing you were trying to hide is gently witnessed and welcomed.
vision.externalJourney: Keen fails to steal honey, is redirected by Aida, visits Bo’s hollow tree, walks him through the woods, helps him arrive at the Learning Circle, and returns home to find Fuzzby attempting his own honey heist.
vision.internalJourney: Bo moves from delaying and controlling every detail to taking a visible step forward with his worry still present, then letting his tail become play instead of proof that something is wrong with him.
vision.relationshipChanges: Bo and Keen shift from strangers at a doorway to easy friends; Bo and Aida move from cautious distance to shared truth; Bo and the Learning Circle group move from imagined judgement to delighted acceptance. Fuzzby and Zenny provide the comic echo: being ridiculous and still belonging.
vision.emotionalCurve: Playful mischief opens the episode, then narrows into Bo’s held-at-the-door worry. The woods give relief through play, dip again at the log, soften through Aida’s honesty, glow into the walk forward, burst into group joy, and settle in a warm, lightly comic garden coda.
vision.comedyCurve: The comedy starts with stealth, snore bubbles, pollen and sneezes; turns into tail-poof escalation and Keen’s useless-tail demonstration; blooms into group delight at the Learning Circle; and ends with Fuzzby’s flower-disguise failure and Zenny’s tiny crack of amusement.
vision.setupPayoffMap: The untouched honeycomb and Fuzzby’s “never ever” return in the final garden heist. Bo’s conker and repeated packing plant his need for control. The tail’s first unwanted poof pays off as a chosen game in the woods and then as the Learning Circle’s delight. Aida’s vision of Bo unable to move pays off in Bo walking forward under pink and blue light. “Every single time” moves from Aida’s truth to Bo’s own action phrase.
vision.visualMotifs: Closed/open thresholds, paws holding objects too tightly, Bo’s tail expanding beyond his control, the forest path as a visible line between home and belonging, and the honeycomb as comic temptation that remains untouched.
vision.sonicMotifs: Crunching steps, snore-bubble pops, sneeze blasts, the shave-and-a-haircut knock, tail POOFs, Aida’s bowl tone, rose and aquamarine glow tones, group cheers, and Zenny’s bookend Ommmm.
vision.climax: Aida and Keen each offer their crystal truth, pink and blue light join on the forest path, and Bo takes one step, then another, toward the Learning Circle.
vision.resolution: At the Learning Circle, Bo’s tail poofs in front of everyone and is met with wonder, cheering and play; later, he draws with Keen while Aida watches his settled belonging from the edge of the clearing.
vision.intendedFinalFeeling: Warm, giggly relief: the child feels the fun of the fluffy tail, while the adult feels the ache of a child being welcomed without needing to edit himself.

northStar.surfaceStory: Fuzzby tries to sneak up on the untouched honeycomb in Keen’s garden by pretending to be a flower, overcommits, gives himself away, tumbles into Keen, then ends the episode tangled in petals while Zenny quietly cracks.
northStar.universalTruth: Sometimes the thing we try to hide makes us most visible — and being lovingly caught can feel safer than getting away with it.

treatments.name: The Garden Catches the Disguise
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience feels the garden itself trying not to giggle. Children read it as a sneaky flower getting betrayed by every tiny twig and petal; adults read the tenderness of a childlike performer making himself more visible the harder he tries to disappear. The suspense is not “will he be punished?” but “how long can this ridiculous disguise pretend it belongs here?”
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: The governing point of view belongs to the environment around the untouched honeycomb. Fuzzby believes he is controlling the scene, but the garden knows the truth first. Keen is the grounded witness who recognizes the earlier sneakiness, and Zenny is the still final judge whose almost-smile confirms affection. Fuzzby’s want is honey and dignity; his need is to be lovingly seen in the mess.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: Environmental participation plus escalating overcommitment. The low twigs, petals, grass and honeycomb are not background; they expose the lie. The comedy turns when the twig snap changes Fuzzby from “secret flower” to “friend caught in costume.” The callback line lands because the environment has already told on him before Keen says it.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Fuzzby performs the disguise with full pomp: chest proud, flower posture too large, flight path too eager to be plant-like, altitude porpoising even when he is trying to seem still. He does not become calm; he tries to force manic bee energy into a fake flower shape, which makes the body funnier. Keen tends the garden with ordinary focus, then his recognition arrives through a visible little thought-chain: interruption, squint, memory, delight, catch. Zenny’s performance is rationed almost to nothing: meditation holds, tiny eye-change, smallest smile/giggle crack, then controlled return to “Ommmm…”
treatments.visualGrammar: The scene is composed as a living garden maze around a forbidden prize. Foreground stems and petals repeatedly partially hide and reveal Fuzzby, making concealment physically real rather than merely acted. The honeycomb remains a warm visual anchor, always tempting but never consumed. Sunset amber begins inviting and becomes comic-exposing as petal colour and tangled shapes disturb the calm.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera behaves like a curious garden creature already suspicious of this “flower.” It discovers Fuzzby through occlusions, lets stems cross him, and allows the frame to be interrupted by the very objects that will catch him. It does not wait safely for the tumble; it lets the twig snap redirect attention, so the audience feels the garden’s betrayal with him.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Movement belongs to Fuzzby and the garden’s little reactions; stillness belongs to the honeycomb, Keen’s grounded tending, and Zenny’s meditation. The joke is that Fuzzby tries to join the still world and cannot. After the tumble, the whole garden settles around him, making his petal-tangled flop the loudest object even when he is barely moving.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Depth carries the story: honeycomb as tempting mid-depth prize, Keen grounded near his work, Fuzzby crossing through obstructing foreground vegetation, Zenny held farther off in calm space. Twigs and petals live close enough to the lens to become comic hazards. The final image must preserve readable geography: honeycomb untouched, Keen’s garden restored, Fuzzby visibly stuck, Zenny’s calm re-established with the trace of her crack still felt.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: Begin with peaceful evening order. Let Fuzzby’s over-disguise introduce a false slow rhythm that keeps getting punctured by tiny environmental betrayals. The twig snap is the sharp turn; the tumble is the release; Keen’s “Never, ever – Fuzzby!” turns exposure into shared memory. Fuzzby’s broken “Ever … Bzzzzz … Ever?” is the aftershock, and Zenny’s two “Ommmm…” lines restore the garden while hiding a giggle inside the calm.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Cuts are motivated by discovery, concealment becoming revelation, impact, and comic punctuation. Avoid automatic reaction coverage. Stay with occluded, evolving frames when the hiding is the joke; cut only when the garden gives new information, when Keen’s recognition changes the power, or when Zenny’s tiny reaction becomes the scene’s final emotional permission.
treatments.openingImage: The untouched honeycomb glowing in low sunset among neat garden life, with one suspiciously overlarge flower-shape not yet fully understood behind the living stems.
treatments.closingImage: A warm wide garden at rest: honeycomb still untouched, petals still tangled around Fuzzby, Keen’s world no longer threatened, and Zenny returned to stillness with the tiniest aftertaste of laughter in the air.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Do not photograph this as a standard sneak-up and fall. The danger is safe garden prettiness with Fuzzby simply entering frame. Make the environment an active comic author: occlude him, catch him, reveal him, and let the honeycomb’s calm embarrass his effort. The opening frame must already contain suspicion and pressure, not a neutral postcard of the garden.

treatments.name: Fuzzby’s Secret Mission Is Too Big for the Frame
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience rides Fuzzby’s self-important thrill and feels the scene almost fail to contain him. Children enjoy the flower-spy who cannot fly like a flower; adults enjoy the familiar panic of trying to look casual while every choice screams the opposite. The laugh comes from being inside his confidence right before the world proves it was nonsense.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: The governing point of view is Fuzzby’s. He believes this is a grand, clever operation; the scene gently reveals it is an obvious, over-built mistake. Keen’s callback is not a scold but the moment Fuzzby realizes he has been seen by someone who understands the exact rhythm of sneakiness. Zenny’s tiny crack gives him permission not to repair his dignity.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: Anticipation to reversal, hiding failure, and status change. Fuzzby enters as self-appointed master of disguise; the twig snap re-titles him instantly as “caught friend in petals.” His attempt to continue the “ever” rhythm from the grass is the cover-up after the crash, and that cover-up is funnier and warmer than the impact.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Fuzzby’s disguise is played with complete seriousness. He makes proud ceremonial pauses that his wings ruin, adjusts himself like a heroic statue while bobbing too high and too low, and treats each near-exposure as proof he must commit harder. After the tumble, the air goes out of the performance but not into shame: dazed, tangled, still trying to preserve the rhythm with “Ever … Bzzzzz … Ever?” before the body chooses the honest flop. Keen is not clever in a superior way; he recognizes a game he once played and catches it with delight. Zenny remains the opposite instrument: almost no movement, almost no smile, maximum meaning.
treatments.visualGrammar: The visual grammar is unstable and subjective around Fuzzby: near-misses, tight passages between garden shapes, abrupt scale shifts between his tiny body and oversized petals. The frame has too little ceiling for his ego and too many edges for his disguise. When the scene hands control to Keen and then Zenny, compositions become steadier and more grounded, so the audience feels Fuzzby’s performance run out of fuel.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera follows and struggles to keep up with Fuzzby rather than waiting for him. It can be briefly fooled by his own confidence, then lose him behind flowers, catch up to the snapped twig, and arrive in the tumble with the same startled energy he has. Once Keen recognizes him, the camera stops flattering the mission and lets the scene see him clearly.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Fuzzby is all manic direction changes and erratic altitude, even while disguised. Keen’s gardening rhythm is steady enough to make Fuzzby’s motion look guiltier. Zenny’s meditation is the final wall of stillness: his leftover buzzing rhythm collapses beside her calm, and her tiny giggle is treated as a major event because everything around it has gone quiet.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Depth is experienced as obstacles in Fuzzby’s path: petals too close, twigs arriving from unexpected planes, the honeycomb always visible enough to lure him onward. The garden’s scale should make him feel tiny but over-important. After the crash, depth opens up so his stuckness is plainly visible and the untouched honeycomb can share the same world as the failed mission without needing explanation.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: Start with mock-ceremonial stealth: Fuzzby trying to make the mission feel grand. Each physical adjustment overcommits the disguise further. The escalation peaks not with the biggest crash but with the smallest sound: the twig snap. Then the scene spills into tumble, callback, dazed attempted recovery, flop, Zenny’s almost-giggle, and the final calm. The rhythm should feel like a balloon loudly trying not to squeak, then gently deflating.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Favor experiential cutting: new visual idea, surprise, impact, altered point of view. Do not cut to explain where everyone is if the motion and garden geography already tell us. Let some entries and exits be imperfect and slightly late so Fuzzby feels genuinely uncontrollable. Once the crash has exposed him, simplify the cutting and allow the quiet reactions to earn their space.
treatments.openingImage: Fuzzby already in motion inside his absurd flower disguise, squeezed by sunset garden stems, with the honeycomb glimpsed ahead like a prize he is dramatically over-preparing to reach.
treatments.closingImage: Fuzzby flattened back into the grass and petals, his grand mission reduced to a soft buzzing question, while the garden has become calm enough for Zenny’s “Ommmm…” to reclaim the evening.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Do not tidy Fuzzby into readable centre-frame flight. If the frame always contains him neatly, we have contradicted his character. Let the camera be outpaced, let the disguise block our view, let the garden edges feel dangerous, but keep the geography clear enough that a young child knows honeycomb, Keen, Fuzzby and Zenny are all part of one comic space.

treatments.name: Zenny’s Calm Gets One Tiny Crack
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience experiences the scene as a peaceful evening meditation gradually invaded by the world’s least convincing flower. Children wait for the silly bee to crash into the calm; adults feel the sweetness of Zenny trying not to laugh because affection is leaking through her discipline. The final pleasure is not that Fuzzby is exposed, but that Zenny lets him belong in her quiet.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: The governing point of view is Zenny’s stillness, even though Fuzzby drives the plot. The scene asks: what does it take to disturb someone who almost never gives anything away? Fuzzby’s need is witnessed through Zenny’s restraint; Keen’s callback makes the mistake safe; Zenny’s tiny giggle makes it loved.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: Movement against stillness, restraint to release, and deadpan observation. Fuzzby’s over-disguise and tumble are the moving storm; Zenny’s meditation is the fixed point. The laugh peaks not at noise but at the tiny breach in her calm. Her return to “Ommmm…” is the comic lid placed back on a pot that has already bubbled over.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Zenny is directed as the scene’s pressure gauge: slow breath, minimal facial change, voice level and soft on both “Ommmm…” lines, with the smallest crack of amusement allowed between them. Fuzzby must earn that crack with full-bodied overcommitment: too proud a flower pose, too frantic a sneak, too much recovery effort after he is clearly tangled. Keen remains warm and immediate; his “Never, ever – Fuzzby!” is recognition, not accusation, with the callback rhythm carrying the affection.
treatments.visualGrammar: The visual grammar begins composed, low, and quiet around Zenny’s meditation space, with garden order and sunset softness. Fuzzby’s intrusion creates diagonals, colour bursts, and petal chaos crossing that calm. The honeycomb is present as the temptation but not the emotional centre; the emotional centre is the distance between Zenny’s still face and Fuzzby’s tangled body.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera is patient with Zenny and opinionated about her restraint. It does not chase every Fuzzby flourish; it allows some of his chaos to invade her calm space, sometimes as sound or partial motion before full visibility. When her tiny smile/giggle happens, the camera treats it as the scene’s true reveal. Fuzzby’s crash is the setup; Zenny’s almost-laugh is the payoff.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Stillness is dominant by design. Fuzzby’s motion must feel like it is repeatedly colliding with a quiet room even though we are outdoors. Keen’s grounded tending gives the scene a second calm rhythm; Fuzzby violates both. After the flop, the scene returns to stillness, but it is not the same stillness: Zenny’s calm now contains warmth and shared absurdity.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Use depth to show calm being invaded: Zenny’s meditation space in one plane, Keen’s garden work in another, Fuzzby’s disguise crossing between them like a bad secret. The honeycomb remains visible enough to rhyme with the opening temptation. Petals and grass around Fuzzby should create a comic nest rather than a humiliating trap; he is caught by softness.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: The rhythm starts slow enough for children to understand “quiet garden.” Fuzzby’s entry adds fussy, over-busy micro-rhythms. The twig snap is a little thunderclap inside meditation. The tumble and callback release the big laugh, then the scene decrescendos into Fuzzby’s dazed rhythm from the grass. Zenny’s first “Ommmm…” tries to restore calm; her tiny giggle betrays her; the second “Ommmm…” restores the surface while preserving the joke underneath.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Hold longer than a conventional gag would whenever restraint is the joke. Cuts should be few and motivated by intrusion into calm, recognition, and the tiny emotional change in Zenny. Avoid automatic cutaways to every action result. If Fuzzby crosses the frame as a disruptive blur or partial petal-shape, that can be stronger than cleanly displaying each step of the sneak.
treatments.openingImage: Zenny’s calm meditation and Keen’s orderly sunset garden share a quiet frame, with the untouched honeycomb glowing nearby and a faintly wrong flower-shape beginning to disturb the peace at the edge of the garden world.
treatments.closingImage: A peaceful wide sunset garden after the disturbance: Zenny back in meditation, Keen’s garden intact, honeycomb untouched, and Fuzzby still petal-stuck close enough to prove the calm has accepted him rather than expelled him.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: The risk is making Zenny a reaction insert after the physical gag. Resist that. Build the whole scene around the value of her stillness, so her tiny smile reads as a major story event. Also resist over-cutting Fuzzby’s tumble; the comedy should invade a calm composition, not become generic slapstick coverage.

treatmentSelection.selectedTreatment: The Garden Catches the Disguise — with Fuzzby’s outpaced-frame pressure borrowed from Treatment 2
combinedFrom: Fuzzby’s Secret Mission Is Too Big for the Frame
treatmentSelection.governingAudienceExperience: The audience feels the garden trying not to giggle as Fuzzby’s over-serious disguise makes him more visible the harder he tries to hide — until being caught turns embarrassment into belonging.
treatmentSelection.rationale: Treatment 1 is the scene truth. It makes the untouched honeycomb, twigs, petals, grass, and sunset garden active comic partners rather than scenery, which matches the signed contract’s pressure: the world catches the disguise before anyone explains it. It also keeps the emotional owner as Fuzzby while allowing Keen to be the warm recogniser and Zenny to be the final tiny permission. The scene’s meaning is clear: the thing Fuzzby hides behind becomes the soft net that lets him be seen safely. Treatment 2 contributes useful energy: Fuzzby’s mission should feel too self-important for the frame, with the camera sometimes outpaced by his overcommitment. That gives the selected treatment more bodily comedy and less postcard prettiness. Treatment 3 has a lovely final instinct for Zenny’s tiny crack, but making Zenny’s stillness the governing point of view shifts the scene away from Fuzzby’s embarrassment-and-belonging arc. Zenny should be the aftertaste, not the engine.
treatmentSelection.rejectionChecks: Selected approach explicitly rejects fixed character lanes: geography is held through honeycomb, garden obstacles, Keen’s grounded tending, Fuzzby’s erratic path, and Zenny’s calm — not permanent screen sides. It rejects keeping all characters visible: occlusion by stems and petals is part of the joke. It rejects habitual action/reaction coverage and repeated close-up punctuation: cuts are only for discovery, exposure, impact, recognition, and Zenny’s final permission. It rejects safe camera placement: the camera is allowed to be interrupted, outpaced, and redirected by the garden. It rejects mechanical shot counts and generic ‘cinematic’ language: the direction is observable — partial reveals, twig catch, petal tangle, honeycomb untouched, Fuzzby flopping instead of repairing pride. Treatment 3 is rejected as governing treatment because it risks making Zenny a structural reaction payoff and demoting Fuzzby’s need to be seen in the mess; we retain only the tiny crack as the closing emotional button. Treatment 2 is not rejected, but subordinated: if used alone, its subjective mission energy could over-flatter Fuzzby’s fantasy and reduce the garden’s authorship.

beats.whatChanges: Fuzzby begins as a self-appointed secret flower approaching the honeycomb and ends as an exposed friend physically caught by the garden and socially caught by Keen’s callback.
beats.whoDrives: The garden drives the exposure through occluding stems, snagging twigs and tangling petals; Fuzzby drives the overcommitment that makes those hazards work; Keen drives the final change from embarrassment to shared recognition.
beats.audienceAnticipation: The audience is ahead of Fuzzby: they can see the disguise is far too eager and wait for the exact tiny thing that will betray him.
beats.actionOrChoice: Fuzzby forces manic bee energy into a fake-flower pose and keeps sneaking after the garden has already made him suspicious; the twig snap becomes the turn, and Keen chooses recognition over scolding.
beats.consequence: The disguise stops protecting Fuzzby and becomes the evidence against him: he tumbles into Keen, the honeycomb remains untouched, and Keen’s locked callback names the game everyone now understands.
beats.emotionalOrComicHandover: The physical crash releases the suspense, and Keen’s line hands the scene to Fuzzby’s dazed aftershock rather than to punishment.

emotionContract.entryState: Hungry, proud, and thrilled by the risk of being clever near the untouched honeycomb.
emotionContract.pressure: The honeycomb is visible and tempting, Keen is present in the garden, and every stem or twig makes the disguise harder to sustain.

emotionContract.exitState: Exposed, tangled, and no longer in control of the story he tried to stage.
emotionContract.observableEvidence: His flight path is too eager to belong to a flower, the twig snap redirects attention, and the tumble lands him against Keen instead of near the honeycomb.
emotionContract.heldAfterBeat: The audience knows Fuzzby has been caught safely, but his pride has not yet found a graceful place to land.

comedyContract.setup: A peaceful evening garden frames the untouched honeycomb as the prize, with Keen grounded in ordinary tending and one over-serious flower-shape trying to pass as scenery.
comedyContract.expectation: Fuzzby expects a grand disguise to make him invisible long enough to get close to the honeycomb.
comedyContract.disruption: The garden refuses to support the lie: foreground stems hide and reveal him, twigs catch the overlarge disguise, and one sharp snap turns secrecy into exposure.
comedyContract.button: Keen’s “42	Never, ever – Fuzzby!” converts the tumble into a callback and lets the audience laugh at recognition, not punishment.
comedyContract.hold: Hold long enough after the line for the untouched honeycomb, the petal mess, and Fuzzby’s failed dignity to be readable in the same comic idea.

physicalStaging.staysVisible: The honeycomb stays readable as the untouched anchor; Keen stays grounded near the garden work; the occluding stems and twig stay visible enough to prove the garden caused the reveal; Fuzzby remains visible through partial concealments rather than appearing from nowhere.
physicalStaging.contactAndWeight: The twig catches the disguise with a clear snag before it snaps; petals and stems drag against Fuzzby’s motion; his tumble has contact into Keen and a soft garden landing, with the environment confirming force through bent stems and disturbed petals.
physicalStaging.payoffShape: A proud fake-flower approach collapses into a petal-tangled crash at Keen’s feet, with the route to the honeycomb visibly failed and the disguise now making Fuzzby more noticeable than before.
prohibitedStaging: Do not make Fuzzby simply enter cleanly into an open frame with no occlusion or garden interference.

Do not let the tumble become weightless spinning without contact, drag, or a readable landing.

performances.speaker: Keen
performances.voiceIdentity: Keen: grounded, practical, caring; the calm bear whose alarm arrives as responsibility, not panic.
performances.dramaticIntention: To stop Fuzzby’s runaway performance and make him feel caught before he can pretend the crash was planned.
performances.subtext: I knew this was you, and I am not letting you wriggle out of it.
performances.relationshipTarget: Fuzzby, collapsed against him; Zenny is present but not the target.
performances.emotionalEntry: Garden-patient and matter-of-fact, mid-tending, not expecting the disguise to become a collision.
performances.emotionalExit: A little winded by the impact, but still firmly in charge of the moment.
performances.pace: Begins unhurried and certain; pivots sharply on the dash as the body-contact lands.
performances.rhythm: Ordinary caretaker rhythm interrupted by one clean crash-beat.
performances.pauses: Let the dash carry the twig-snap/tumble arrival; no extra comic pause before the name.
performances.breaths: Small inhale on the impact before “Fuzzby,” more caught than frightened.
performances.nonVerbalActions: Keep the voice connected to the raised paw: Keen does not spin into panic; the line caps the crash from stillness.
performances.physicalActionRelationship: The voice supports the body’s calm authority: Fuzzby’s chaos lands against Keen’s stillness, and Keen’s naming finishes the gag.
performances.expectedTiming: Do not start at frame one. Begin after the quiet tending beat is established; “Never, ever” during the calm recognition, dash over the snap/tumble landing, “Fuzzby!” on the short still contact.

performances.speaker: Fuzzby
performances.voiceIdentity: Fuzzby: over-the-top show-off energy deflating into sheepish, fuzzy resilience; he tries to turn failure into a bit even when flattened.
performances.dramaticIntention: To convince Keen and Zenny that he can still make this look intentional, while secretly asking if anyone is buying it.
performances.subtext: Please let that count as clever, because I have no dignity left.
performances.relationshipTarget: Keen first, then Zenny as the hoped-for amused witness.
performances.emotionalEntry: Dazed aftershock; the grand disguise performance has leaked out of him.
performances.emotionalExit: A tiny, embarrassed hope survives under the flop and weak thumbs-up.
performances.pace: Loose, delayed, underpowered; each phrase arrives as if his thoughts are catching up with his petals.
performances.rhythm: Broken three-part wobble: attempt, buzz-collapse, hopeful question.
performances.pauses: The first ellipsis is his system rebooting; the second is the flop landing before he risks the question.
performances.breaths: A deflated exhale before the first word; the buzz should ride on leftover air, not fresh confidence.
performances.nonVerbalActions: Let the voice sag with the backward flop; the final “Ever?” barely lifts with the slack thumbs-up.
performances.physicalActionRelationship: The voice surrenders with the body: no pomp left, only a faint comic afterimage of the disguise routine.
performances.expectedTiming: Start after the soft landing stillness. “Ever” on the weak attempt to answer, “Bzzzzz” as the flop goes back, final “Ever?” with the tiny paw gesture lagging behind it.

performances.speaker: Zenny
performances.voiceIdentity: Zenny: serene, minimal, dryly amused without chasing the joke; stillness is her comic timing.
performances.dramaticIntention: To let Fuzzby know she saw everything and is amused, without surrendering her calm completely.
performances.subtext: That was ridiculous, and I love that you committed to it.
performances.relationshipTarget: Fuzzby, from her leaf; Keen is included only as part of the shared garden stillness.
performances.emotionalEntry: Composed meditation, almost untouched by the crash.
performances.emotionalExit: A tiny crack of warmth and amusement slips through before she gathers herself again.
performances.pace: Very slow, held on a single relaxed out-breath; no punchline push.
performances.rhythm: Smooth meditation tone with the smallest smile audible near the end.
performances.pauses: The ellipsis lets the sound taper rather than stop; hold just long enough for the eye-open and smile to read.
performances.breaths: One settled breath in before the line; keep the breath quiet and centred.
performances.nonVerbalActions: The voice should match the rationed movement: one eye opens, smile appears, a tiny giggle nearly escapes.
performances.physicalActionRelationship: The voice gently contradicts full stillness for one beat: calm remains the frame, amusement is the small ripple.
performances.expectedTiming: Delay until after Fuzzby’s weak gesture has landed. Begin as Zenny opens one eye; let the soft laugh sit on the smile, then release back toward stillness.

performances.speaker: Zenny
performances.voiceIdentity: Zenny: serene, economical, amused only as much as the garden can absorb; her calm is active, not sleepy.
performances.dramaticIntention: To restore the garden’s quiet and gently invite Fuzzby’s chaos to settle with her.
performances.subtext: Funny happened; now we can all breathe again.
performances.relationshipTarget: Fuzzby and the garden together; she is not correcting him, just absorbing the aftershock.
performances.emotionalEntry: A tiny giggle has just passed through her composure.
performances.emotionalExit: Returned to stillness, with a trace of fondness left in the air.
performances.pace: Even slower than the first, longer and lower in energy, resolving rather than teasing.
performances.pauses: The ellipsis is the tableau easing into quiet; do not add a separate pause after it.
performances.breaths: Begin on a controlled, comfortable exhale following a small contented sigh.
performances.nonVerbalActions: As her eye closes again, the voice closes the little door that opened for the giggle.
performances.physicalActionRelationship: The voice completes the body’s return to stillness; the final wide should feel held, not announced.
performances.expectedTiming: Enter after the giggle/smile has had a clean read. Let this second “Ommmm…” carry the frame into the quiet final tableau.

orderedEvents.text: Keen tends to his garden. Golden sunset. The honeycomb still sits untouched.

FUZZBY sneaks through the grass wearing a FLOWER DISGUISE — petals around his head like he's trying to blend in. He freezes, pretending to be a flower. Nothing happens. He peeks around. Creeps toward the honey. A twig SNAPs.
He freezes. Moves again … Trips into a BUZZ-CRASH AND TUMBLES HEAD OVER HEELS TOWRDS KEEN. He face-plants into Keen's back. Keen does not turn around. He simply raises one paw.

orderedEvents.speaker: Keen
orderedEvents.text: 42	Never, ever – Fuzzby!

orderedEvents.text: Ever … Bzzzzz … Ever?
Fuzzby FLOPS backwards still dazed.

orderedEvents.text: 43	Ommmm…

showrunnerJudgement: Pass. I tried to break this on the usual Crystal Bears failures — safe sneak coverage, decorative garden prettiness, automatic reaction cutting, and a coda that explains the feeling — but the scene holds its signed experience. The garden is not just a location: the occluding stems, snagging twig, disturbed petals and untouched honeycomb all participate in exposing Fuzzby. Fuzzby’s want is clear without explanation, his over-disguise makes him more visible, and the crash/callback turns embarrassment into belonging rather than punishment. Keen remains the grounded witness instead of becoming a scold, and Zenny’s minimal crack is correctly treated as final permission, not a reaction-shot punchline. The honeycomb staying untouched in both opening and closing gives the joke its emotional rhyme: nobody wins the trick, but everyone belongs in the mess.
treatmentComparison: The storyboard preserves the selected treatment’s central experience: the audience should feel the garden trying not to giggle. The visual grammar follows the contract by discovering Fuzzby through foreground obstruction rather than presenting a neutral garden postcard or a standard sneak-up/fall. The twig snap is positioned as the garden’s betrayal, not random slapstick. The camera relationship stays curious and garden-held, and the final geography keeps the honeycomb, Keen’s restored order, Fuzzby’s petal-tangled flop, and Zenny’s re-established calm in relationship. The scene also keeps the adult door alive: Fuzzby’s failed dignity is met by recognition and affection, not humiliation. The important beats remain readable muted through staging — the suspicious flower-shape creeping toward the untouched honeycomb, the twig catching/snapping, the tumble into Keen, and Zenny’s tiny stillness-break can all land without relying on dialogue.

The boundary is also a real dramatic boundary: S8.SH1 carries the active sneak/snap/tumble/callback mechanism, while S8.SH2 carries the deflated aftershock, Zenny’s restrained crack, and the final held wide. This is not an avoidable join under 30 seconds, and it protects the shift from physical escalation to quiet comic settling. Both units are short, but not padded; each has a distinct job and usable handoff logic.
